title: Trentino-Alto Adige
quiz.0.question: According to DNA research, what is the “Traminer” grown for centuries in Termeno/Tramin actually?
quiz.0.explanation: Traminer was long thought to originate in Termeno/Tramin, but the grape grown there for centuries is actually Savagnin Blanc; Gewürztraminer is its aromatic, pink-berried mutation (Savagnin Rose). Today only Gewürztraminer is grown in Alto Adige.
quiz.1.question: Which production method is used for Trento DOC?
quiz.1.explanation: Trento DOC covers all traditional method (Metodo Classico) sparkling wines made in Trentino. Created in 1993, it was the first Italian DOC dedicated exclusively to traditional method sparkling wine.
quiz.2.question: Which is Trentino’s most representative red grape?
quiz.2.explanation: Teroldego, the “Prince of Trentino”, is Trentino’s most important red grape and is native to the Campo Rotaliano; Teroldego Rotaliano DOC is 100% Teroldego.
quiz.3.question: Which empire did Alto Adige belong to before 1919?
quiz.3.explanation: Alto Adige was acquired by the House of Habsburg in the 14th century and remained linked to Austria until the end of World War I; it was ceded to the Kingdom of Italy in 1919.
slides.0.title: 🏔️ Trentino-Alto Adige
slides.0.subtitle: A bilingual wine region beneath the Alps
slides.1.title: 🗺️ A Region with Two Identities
slides.1.content:
Alto Adige (Südtirol)

Upper Adige / South Tyrol

Language: officially bilingual, with German as the principal language

Culture: Tyrolean since the 12th century; its people see themselves as Tyrolean

Altitude: hillside vineyards at about 200-1,000 m

Style: elegant, aromatic, age-worthy whites; reds mainly from Schiava, Lagrein and Pinot Nero

Signature grapes: Pinot Bianco, Sauvignon, Gewürztraminer, Sylvaner

Trentino

Trentino

Language: Italian

Culture: once under Austrian rule, but always Italian in language and mindset

Altitude: 200-300 m on the valley floor, up to 800-1,000 m on the slopes

Style: traditional method sparkling wine, Chardonnay and Pinot Grigio, Teroldego reds

Signature wines: Trento DOC, Teroldego Rotaliano DOC

💡 The two autonomous provinces became part of the Kingdom of Italy after World War I (1919); after World War II they were combined into a single region, but the two never truly integrated. Alto Adige is Italy’s northernmost wine region.
slides.2.title: 📜 Trentino’s History and the Edmund Mach Institute (IWS)
slides.2.content:
From an Etruscan amphora to a Roman ban

The carbon dating of an ancient Etruscan wine amphora has proven that viticulture existed in Trentino as early as the 7th century BC, well before the Romans took control of the area in the 1st century BC. The Romans founded Tridentum (modern-day Trento) as an outpost, and it has been the region’s political and economic centre ever since. Commercial ties with Rome remained strong until 92 AD, when Emperor Domitian forbade the Empire’s northern regions to export wine to the south of the Italian peninsula — which prompted local growers to send their wines north of the Alps, beginning Trentino’s long trade with Central Europe. Barbarian invasions destroyed the vineyards, and viticulture only rebounded in the Middle Ages under the monastic orders. The main markets became the German regions of Bavaria and Swabia, which even acquired vineyards in Trentino to secure a steady supply; the most sought-after wines were made from the local Teroldego, Marzemino and Schiava.

In 1027 Trentino became a partially autonomous ecclesiastical principality under the Bishop of Trento, until control passed to the Austrian House of Habsburg. Conquered by Napoléon in the early 19th century, it was returned to Austria in 1815 and incorporated into South Tyrol; in 1919, after World War I, it was annexed by the Kingdom of Italy in recognition of its Italian culture and language, and after World War II it was combined with Alto Adige to form the autonomous region of Trentino-Alto Adige

Istituto Agrario di San Michele all'Adige (Fondazione Edmund Mach)

In 1874 the Tyrolean Parliament opened an agricultural school and research centre in a former Augustinian monastery at San Michele all'Adige; its first director, Edmund Mach, was instrumental in its foundation. It was the first school and experimental station dedicated to viticulture and oenology in Trentino (and one of the first in Italy), and it remains one of Italy’s most advanced and internationally respected wine research centres, hosting the most important Italian ampelographic collection. The estate includes a winery, a distillery and about 120 ha of vines and apple orchards; since 2008 it has been part of the Edmund Mach Foundation

slides.4.title: 🏛️ History and Cultural Heritage
slides.4.content:
From the Rhaeti to today: more than two thousand years of wine

Antiquity

🏺 Before and after Rome

The Rhaeti, an ancient Alpine people of Etruscan origin, grew vines long before the Romans conquered the area in 15 BC. According to Pliny the Elder, the Rhaeti held wine in high regard and used wooden vessels (forerunners of the modern barrel) to store and transport it. From the 11th century Alto Adige was jointly ruled by the Bishops of Trento and Bressanone.

Middle Ages

⛪ Monasteries revive viticulture

Monks and monasteries revived viticulture in the Middle Ages, fuelled by demand from the German-speaking regions to the north; Bavarian and Franconian monasteries even bought vineyards and wineries in Alto Adige. The Abbazia di Novacella in the Valle Isarco still makes wine today.

Austrian era

🦅 The County of Tyrol and the Habsburgs

Between the 12th and 13th centuries Alto Adige was gradually incorporated into the County of Tyrol, then acquired by the House of Habsburg in the 14th century, remaining linked to Austria until the end of World War I. Trentino’s period under Austrian rule was comparatively brief.

Turning point

🇮🇹 Joining Italy (1919)

After World War I the region was ceded to the Kingdom of Italy; briefly annexed to the Third Reich during World War II, it returned to Italy afterwards and was granted considerable autonomy to ease separatist tensions.

Sparkling wine

🍾 The birth of Ferrari (1902)

Giulio Ferrari, an oenologist at the San Michele all'Adige agrarian institute, saw Trentino’s potential for growing Chardonnay for bottle-fermented sparkling wine and founded the Ferrari sparkling house; other producers followed, turning Trentino into a major Italian sparkling wine centre.

DOC era

🏆 Trento DOC is created (1993)

Trento DOC was Italy’s first DOC dedicated exclusively to traditional method sparkling wine, covering all such wines made in Trentino.

🌍 Two characters

🏔️ Alto Adige

  • German-speaking; labels are often in German first, then Italian
  • The strongest self-government of Italy’s five autonomous regions
  • The only region where Italian is not the primary language
  • Described as “a country within a country”
+

🇮🇹 Trentino

  • Always Italian in language and mindset
  • A “Teutonic” responsiveness to market demand
  • Over 80% of its wine is DOC
  • Cooperatives make about three-quarters of production
=

🍇 What they share

  • Alpine landscape and the Dolomites
  • The Pergola Trentina training system
  • A wine industry led by cooperatives
  • Traditional farmsteads both called “maso”

📌 Südtirol / Alto Adige

German: Südtirol (South Tyrol)
Italian: Alto Adige (Upper Adige)
On labels: often bilingual, “Alto Adige/Südtirol”. The province is officially bilingual, with German the principal language in speech and print; Ladin is also spoken in some valleys.
slides.5.title: 🍇 Alto Adige’s Main White Grapes
slides.5.content:
#1

Pinot Grigio

Alto Adige’s second most planted grape (after Schiava), mostly made in stainless steel with little or no oak.

Style: crisp, subtly aromatic
#2

Gewürztraminer

Not native but traditional, and the third most planted grape. Its historic home is Termeno/Tramin and Cortaccia on the west side of the Bassa Atesina.

Style: rose petal, lychee, spice, tropical fruit — fresher and less opulent than elsewhere
#3

Pinot Bianco

Grown here since at least the 1850s; Alto Adige makes world-class Pinot Bianco, best in Oltradige (especially Appiano) and Val d'Adige.

Style: apple, high acidity, finesse; nutty complexity with age
#4

Sauvignon

Called simply “Sauvignon” locally, it is one of Italy’s best Sauvignon Blancs; Terlano is considered its historic home.

Style: intense, mineral, crisp — gooseberry, cut grass, ripe yellow and exotic fruit
#5

Sylvaner

Grown mainly on high-altitude terraces in the Valle Isarco, which holds 95% of Italy’s Sylvaner plantings.

Style: high minerality, pure aromas, earthy, long-lived
slides.6.title: 🏔️ Alto Adige in Depth
slides.6.content:
🌟 Why is it one of Italy’s best white wine regions?

🧭

Italy’s northernmost region

Set in the Alps of north-east Italy, bordering Austria. Despite lying deep in the mountains, it does not have a full alpine climate: caught between the Alps and the Mediterranean climate to the south, it is continental, with a mitigating influence from Lake Garda.

☀️

Sunshine and diurnal swings

About 300 days of sunshine a year, an average growing-season temperature of around 18°C and steady breezes that offset humidity; wide day-night swings give slow ripening and full aromatic development.

⛰️

Hillside vineyards

Only 15% of the land is cultivable and the valley floors are mostly apple orchards, so vineyards lie largely on slopes at 200-1,000 m; hillsides generally give smaller quantities of higher-quality fruit.

🪨

Diverse soils

Volcanic porphyry (Bolzano, Merano, Caldaro)
Weathered schist, gneiss and slate (Valle Isarco, partly Val Venosta)
Limestone and dolomite (Bassa Atesina)
Poor sandy soils (Val Venosta)

📍 The six sub-zones (IWS)

Alto Adige/Südtirol DOC has six sub-zones (all formerly separate DOCs) that may follow the main name on the label: Terlano, Valle Isarco, Santa Maddalena, Colli di Bolzano, Valle Venosta and Meranese. The region has more than 13,000 acres/5,300 ha of vineyards, divided into seven winegrowing districts (Bassa Atesina, Oltradige, Bolzano, Val d'Adige, Merano, Valle Isarco, Val Venosta).

🍷 Santa Maddalena/St. Magdalener

Location: the slopes north of Bolzano

Speciality: Schiava

Considered the historic home of Schiava and its most prestigious zone; the wines are fuller and more structured than other Schiava appellations, and the smaller historic area around Santa Maddalena may add Classico/Klassisch.

🌊 Lago di Caldaro/Kalterersee DOC

Location: around Lake Caldaro in southern Oltradige

Speciality: Schiava (min. 85%)

A separate DOC shared with Trentino but mostly in Alto Adige, producing the largest quantity of Schiava in the region; the wines are light, quaffable and refreshing. The historic area around the lake may add classico/klassisch.

✨ Terlano/Terlaner

Location: around the town of Terlano in the Val d'Adige

Speciality: Sauvignon, Pinot Bianco and other whites

Considered the historic home of Sauvignon; Riserva must age at least 2 years. Wines from Terlano, Nalles and Andriano may use Classico/Klassisch. The local cooperative Cantina Terlano is famous for age-worthy whites.

❄️ Valle Isarco/Eisacktaler

Location: Italy’s most northerly appellation

Speciality: Sylvaner, Kerner, Müller Thurgau, Pinot Grigio

Almost entirely white, from high-altitude, mostly south-facing sites. Wines from around Bressanone/Brixen may add Bressanone/Brixner; Klausner Laitacher is the only red allowed (a blend of Schiava, Lagrein, Portugieser and Pinot Nero). The Abbazia di Novacella is here.

🏛️ Colli di Bolzano/Bozner Leiten

Location: the hills around Bolzano

Speciality: Schiava

A sub-zone dedicated to Schiava. Note: the finest Lagrein comes from the flat, gravelly-sandy plain around Gries within the Bolzano district.

🍏 Valle Venosta/Vinschgau

Location: the north-western extension of the Adige Valley; the newest sub-zone

Speciality: Riesling, Kerner, Müller Thurgau, Pinot Nero

Once dedicated to apple orchards, now a centre of new vineyard development. A cool, dry meso-climate and poor sandy soils give steely, high-acid whites; Riserva must age at least 2 years.

🏘️ Meranese/Meraner

Location: the hills around Merano/Meran

Speciality: Schiava

A sub-zone dedicated to Schiava.

⚖️ The Alto Adige/Südtirol appellation framework

🏆 Alto Adige/Südtirol DOC

Most of the region’s wines fall under this regional DOC; apart from traditional method sparkling wines and Alto Adige Bianco, all must be varietally labelled, with at least 85% of the stated variety. Two-variety white blends are allowed (Pinot Bianco and/or Pinot Nero, Chardonnay-Pinot Bianco, Chardonnay-Pinot Grigio). Except Schiava and Müller Thurgau, wines may be released as Riserva after 2 years of ageing.

🍾 Spumante Metodo Classico

Made from Pinot Bianco and/or Pinot Nero, with at least 15 months on the lees before disgorging; Riserva must age at least 36 months.

🌊 Lago di Caldaro/Kalterersee DOC

Shared with Trentino, with at least 85% Schiava; wines made entirely in Alto Adige may add “Alto Adige/Südtirol”.

🗺️ Valdadige/Etschtaler DOC

An inter-regional DOC shared by Alto Adige, Trentino and Veneto, mainly for Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Grigio and Schiava.

🏭 Led by cooperatives: cooperatives make almost 80% of Alto Adige/Südtirol’s wine; they are more numerous but smaller than in Trentino, and rank not only among Italy’s best cooperatives but among its best wineries. Alto Adige makes less than 1% of Italy’s wine yet has one of the highest proportions of DOC wine.

📊 Most widely planted grapes (Consorzio Tutela Vini Alto Adige/Südtirol, 2017)

Schiava 14% · Pinot Grigio 12% · Gewürztraminer 11% · Pinot Bianco 10% · Chardonnay 10% · Lagrein 8% · Pinot Nero 8% · Sauvignon Blanc 7% · Müller Thurgau 4% · Others 14%

🌸 Traminer and Gewürztraminer

The traditional view: Traminer has long been thought to originate in the town of Termeno/Tramin

DNA research: the grape grown here for centuries is actually Savagnin Blanc, native to north-east France and south-west Germany; Gewürztraminer is its aromatic, pink-berried mutation, Savagnin Rose

🍇 In Alto Adige: only Gewürztraminer is grown; its historic home is Termeno and Cortaccia on the west side of the Bassa Atesina
🌹 Style: rose petal, lychee, spice and tropical fruit, with the variety’s typical high alcohol and rich texture
❄️ Hallmark: fresher and less opulent than elsewhere; vendemmia tardiva (late-harvest) versions are also made

🍷 Oak use depends on the grape

How Alto Adige whites are made

GrapeTypical practice
Small new oakChardonnayBarrel fermentation, lees stirring and oak ageing give riper fruit and sweet spice
Large old casksPinot BiancoSome are fermented or aged in old, neutral casks for a soft, creamy texture
Stainless steelSauvignon, Pinot GrigioMostly stainless steel, with little or no oak
Single vineyardsAll grapesSingle-vineyard bottlings are among the best wines today, expressing diverse terroirs
slides.7.title: 🍇 Native and Distinctive Grapes in Depth
slides.7.content:
🍷 Red grapes in depth

🔴 Teroldego (the Prince of Trentino)

Native

Origin: native to the Campo Rotaliano (Rotaliano Plain) at the northern tip of the Valdadige. First mentioned in the 14th century, it only became popular from the 18th century, mainly in Austria.

DNA: related to Dureza (a parent of Syrah); Lagrein is an offspring of Teroldego.

🎨 Characteristics and style:
  • Colour: deep
  • Aromas: ripe berry fruit, flowers, tar, spice, herbs
  • Palate: intensely fruity and refreshing, dense texture, round tannins
  • Ageing: with controlled yields it makes distinctive, age-worthy wines; the best benefit from bottle age
  • Oak: handles oak well

👑 The pioneer:
In the 1980s Elisabetta Foradori showed the grape’s potential through massal selection, lower yields and Guyot training, and other producers followed.

🔴 Lagrein (native to Alto Adige)

Alto Adige native

Origin: an offspring of Teroldego. The finest Lagrein comes from the flat, gravelly-sandy plain around Gries in the Bolzano district; in Trentino it is mostly planted in the north along the Alto Adige border.

🍷 Two styles:
Lagrein Kretzer (rosé)

Rosé Lagrein is usually labelled Kretzer and is particularly prized

Lagrein Dunkel (dark)

One of the highest anthocyanin levels of any Italian red, so very dark; full-bodied, high in tannin and acidity, often with a bitter finish; berry and violet aromas, with a savoury, meaty character balanced by intense fruit

⚠️ Hard to grow: prone to poor flowering and pollination, needs plenty of warmth, and gives irregular yields.

🍷 Schiava/Vernatsch (a traditional Alto Adige grape)

Traditional

Where: grown in Alto Adige since at least the Middle Ages and believed native there, it is still the most planted “variety”. In Trentino it made up 40% of plantings until the 1970s and still covers more than 300 ha.

🎨 Characteristics and style:
  • Traditional style: light, simple, refreshing reds, once exported in large volumes to German-speaking countries
  • Exports: in steady decline since the 1980s
  • Santa Maddalena: its most prestigious zone, with fuller, more structured wines

🏆 Schiava appellations: Alto Adige Schiava, Santa Maddalena, Meranese, Colli di Bolzano (the last three are Alto Adige sub-zones), Lago di Caldaro DOC and Valdadige Schiava DOC.

🍇 A family of grapes: Schiava is not a single variety but a group of unrelated varieties with similar traits, mainly Grossa, Gentile and Grigia, usually interplanted, with Grossa dominant. In German it is “Vernatsch” (from the Latin sclavus, for vines tied to poles rather than left to climb trees); in most of Germany and Austria it is “Trollinger”, and in Württemberg “Urban”.

🍇 Marzemino (a traditional Trentino grape)

Traditional

Where: native to the Vallagarina, documented since the 14th century and very popular locally; the best come from around Ziresi and Isera.

🎨 Characteristics: a late-ripening grape making fresh, light- to medium-bodied, soft reds with violet, sour cherry, plum, almond and herbs, usually with a slightly bitter finish

🎭 Cultural note: in Mozart’s opera Don Giovanni: “Versa il vino! Eccellente Marzemino!” (Pour the wine! Excellent Marzemino!).

🥂 White grapes in detail

🍾 Chardonnay

Trentino: the most planted grape, introduced in the late 19th century for traditional method sparkling wine
Alto Adige: made both fresh and unoaked and in a barrel-aged style
Trento DOC: usually the dominant grape

🌸 Pinot Grigio

Trentino: slightly less planted than Chardonnay but with the largest total yields; uncomplicated, crisp and light
Alto Adige: the second most planted grape

🍏 Nosiola

Identity: an ancient grape native to Trentino, dating back at least to the 15th century
Use: Vino Santo in the Valle dei Laghi; dry versions are light, with lemon and green hazelnut

🌿 Müller Thurgau

Identity: Riesling × Madeleine Royale
Trentino: the high terraces of Val di Cembra (around Faedo) give exciting wines with flowers and herbs
Alto Adige: on the steep slopes of Valle Isarco and Val Venosta, with a hint of nutmeg

🍐 Pinot Bianco/Weissburgunder

Alto Adige: world-class — apple, high acidity, finesse and elegance
Trentino: grown since the 19th century for still wines and, to a lesser extent, sparkling

🌼 Moscato Giallo

Identity: a long-established grape in Trentino-Alto Adige, often confused with Moscato Bianco
Style: more floral and spicy, without the overt grapiness; made dry and sweet
Trentino: at its best around Besenello

🧊 Sylvaner

Where: the high terraces of the Valle Isarco
Status: 95% of Italy’s Sylvaner
Style: high minerality, pure aromas, earthy, long-lived

🌼 Kerner

Identity: a German cross of Riesling × Schiava (Trollinger)
Where: high sites in the Valle Isarco and Val Venosta
Style: fragrant, fruity, spicy

📊 Red grapes compared

LagreinBolzano (Gries)FullHigh tannin/high acidityAlto Adige LagreinDark, violet, bitter finish

slides.8.title: 🍷 The Pride of Trentino
slides.8.content:
Traditional method sparkling

Trento DOC

Method: traditional method (Metodo Classico), second fermentation in bottle

Grapes: mainly Chardonnay and Pinot Nero, usually led by Chardonnay; Pinot Bianco and/or Meunier may be added

Time on lees: at least 15 months non-vintage, 24 months vintage (millesimato), 36 months Riserva

Vineyards: on slopes up to 800 m

Status: Trentino’s “mountain bubbles”, considered among Italy’s finest traditional method sparkling wines

Created in 1993 — Italy’s first DOC dedicated to traditional method sparkling wine
Native red grape

Teroldego Rotaliano DOC

Grape: 100% Teroldego

Area: the Campo Rotaliano north of Trento, a gravelly, sandy plain between Mezzocorona, Mezzolombardo and San Michele all'Adige

Style: dark, fruity and savoury, with ripe berry fruit, flowers, tar and spice

Riserva: aged at least 2 years; a rosato (or Kretzer) is also made

Status: Trentino’s best red and one of the most distinctive reds of northern Italy

Its quality revival was led by Elisabetta Foradori in the 1980s
slides.9.title: 🍇 More Trentino Grapes and Industry Data (IWS)
slides.9.content:
Plantings by grape (Consorzio Vini Trentino, 2014)

Chardonnay 28% · Pinot Grigio 27% · Müller Thurgau 9% · Teroldego 6% · Merlot 6% · Traminer Aromatico 4% · Marzemino 3% · Schiava 3% · Others 14%. White grapes now make up almost 70% of Trentino’s plantings — the result of a complete switch in the 1980s, in response to market demand, from a region historically focused on reds from Schiava, Marzemino and Enantio.

🍇 The Grappa tradition: Trentino has been renowned for centuries for Grappa (a spirit distilled from pomace); the vinacce used must all come from Trentino, and the spirit is acclaimed for its smoothness, freshness and delicate fruit

Other native and traditional grapes: Enantio, Moscato Giallo, Rebo, Casetta

Enantio: native to the Vallagarina and formerly called “Lambrusco a Foglia Frastagliata” (though unrelated to the Lambrusco family); it fell out of favour after phylloxera and has recently been revived, making juicy wines with bright acidity, red berries and herbs
Moscato Giallo (Yellow Muscat): a long-established grape in Trentino-Alto Adige, often confused with Moscato Bianco but more floral and spicy, without the overt grapiness; at its best around Besenello, it makes dry and sweet wines with honey, tropical fruit and sweet spice
Other red grapes: Rebo (a Merlot × Teroldego cross) and Casetta; another white grape is Manzoni Bianco
slides.10.title: 🗺️ The Sub-zones of Trentino DOC (IWS)
slides.10.content:
As of 2017, Trentino has 8 DOCs

Trentino DOC is the region’s most important catch-all appellation, with Chardonnay and Pinot Grigio making up more than half its production; wines meeting stricter criteria (specific vineyard positions and altitude, planting density, maximum yield, alcohol and minimum ageing) may be labelled superiore; riserva requires at least 1 year of ageing for whites and 2 years for reds.

Marzemino sub-zones

Under Trentino DOC, Marzemino may only come from the southern Adige Valley (the Vallagarina). The Isera sub-zone produces a more complex and refined Marzemino Superiore; the Ziresi sub-zone (“cherry trees” in the local dialect), around Volano and Calliano, produces one of the richest, fullest-bodied Marzeminos in Trentino

Other official sub-zones

Castel Beseno: dedicated to Moscato Giallo in dry, late-harvest and passito styles | Sorni: a small area north of Trento; the rosso blends Teroldego, Schiava and Lagrein, and the bianco blends Nosiola, Müller Thurgau, Pinot Bianco and Chardonnay, among others
Valle di Cembra (added in 2016): the steep terraces of purple porphyritic rock in the Cembra Valley, some at 2,800 ft/850 m; varietal Müller Thurgau, Riesling, Schiava, Schiava Gentile and Pinot Nero are allowed, with Müller Thurgau considered the most distinctive

Vino Santo rules

Nosiola grapes are air-dried on graticci in high, well-ventilated rooms through which the Ora del Garda breeze passes; drying can last 5-6 months, during which the grapes are affected by noble rot, and vinification can take 2-3 years to reach 12-13% abv. The wine must age at least 3 years (most producers age it 7-10 years). Vino Santo Superiore is stricter: longer drying, higher minimum potential alcohol and at least 4 years of ageing. The name “Vino Santo” (holy wine) is believed to come from the tradition of pressing the dried grapes during Holy Week
slides.11.title: 🗺️ Other Appellations and the Wine Industry (IWS)
slides.11.content:
Trentino’s minor DOCs

Casteller DOC: a red-only appellation requiring at least 50% Merlot, with the balance from Schiava and/or Enantio and/or Teroldego and/or Lagrein; Schiava is usually the main blending component
Lago di Caldaro (Caldaro) DOC: red wine from Schiava, an appellation shared with Alto Adige, where most of its area actually lies
Valdadige Terradeiforti (Terradeiforti) DOC: an inter-regional DOC shared with Veneto, covering Trentino’s south-west corner though most of its area lies in Veneto; varietal Enantio, Casetta and Pinot Grigio

Inter-regional IGT / DOC

Vigneti delle Dolomiti IGT: an inter-regional IGT covering Trentino, Veneto and the Belluno province; Trentino’s most important IGT by volume and quality, including Bordeaux blends from top producers (such as the Bordeaux-style blend pioneered by Tenuta San Leonardo since the early 1980s) and high-quality varietal Teroldego, Cabernet Sauvignon, Nosiola, Manzoni Bianco, Chardonnay and Müller Thurgau
Delle Venezie DOC: an inter-regional DOC covering Trentino, Veneto and Friuli Venezia Giulia, focused on varietal Pinot Grigio (labelled Pinot Grigio delle Venezie DOC); the wines are sound and fruity, though sometimes at the expense of Trentino’s terroir

An industry led by cooperatives

Cooperatives dominate Trentino’s wine industry, making nearly 75% (three-quarters) of production! Unlike most Italian cooperatives, created by the central government to subsidise growers or stabilise the farm economy, Trentino’s growers organised independently and from a position of strength in the early 1900s to better serve local and northern export markets
Since the late 20th century, more and more growers aware of their terroir’s potential have bottled their own wine instead of selling grapes to the cooperatives, steadily increasing the number of small fine-wine estates; these formed associations such as Vignaioli del Trentino and I Dolomitici to raise quality, which in turn pushed cooperatives to make distinctive single-vineyard wines too. The Consorzio di Tutela Vini del Trentino represents over 90% of Trentino’s producers and growers
💡 Maso: in Trentino and Alto Adige the traditional rural homestead is called a “maso”, a word also used for estate wineries
slides.12.title: 🍾 Trento DOC in Depth
slides.12.content:
📜 The history of Trento DOC

Late 19th c.

Chardonnay arrives

Chardonnay was introduced to Trentino in the late 19th century to make traditional method sparkling wine, and is now Trentino’s most planted grape.

1902

Giulio Ferrari founds Ferrari

Giulio Ferrari, an oenologist at the San Michele all'Adige agrarian institute, saw Trentino’s potential for growing Chardonnay for bottle-fermented sparkling wine and founded the Ferrari sparkling house.

20th c.

A sparkling wine centre

Within a few decades other producers joined, making Trentino a major Italian sparkling wine centre. Ferrari was later run by the Lunelli family.

1993

Trento DOC is created

Trento DOC was created to cover all of Trentino’s traditional method sparkling wines — Italy’s first DOC dedicated exclusively to traditional method sparkling wine.

👑 What makes the “mountain bubbles” special

🍾

Traditional method

The same Metodo Classico as Champagne and Franciacorta: second fermentation in bottle; riddling may be manual or mechanical.

⛰️

Hillside vineyards

The area roughly matches Trentino DOC, with vineyards on slopes up to 800 m.

🌙

Wide diurnal swings

Cold air descends from the peaks each evening, creating wide day-night swings that preserve the grapes’ natural acidity.

⏳

Time on lees

At least 15 months for non-vintage, 24 months for vintage and 36 months for Riserva.

slides.13.title: 🏔️ The Advantages of a Mountain Terroir
slides.13.content:
🏔️

Mountain barrier

The mountains block cold northerly winds and the Dolomites to the north-east protect the whole region; altitude tempers summer heat, suiting aromatic varieties.

🌙

Wide diurnal swings

Cold air descends from the peaks each evening, blanketing the vineyards and creating wide swings that preserve natural acidity.

🌊

Lake Garda and the Ora del Garda

Lake Garda moderates temperatures in the south in summer and winter; the Ora del Garda blows north every day during daylight, cooling the vineyards and lowering humidity inland.

🪨

Varied soils

Trentino is mainly dolomite, limestone, granite and volcanic porphyry; Alto Adige has porphyry, schist, gneiss, limestone and sandy soils — hence its range of styles.
slides.14.title: 🗺️ Sub-regions and Meso-climates
slides.14.content:
🏞️ Trentino’s four main valleys

🌾 The Valdadige and Campo Rotaliano

Location: the Adige Valley is the largest valley by size and production, with the Campo Rotaliano in the north and the Vallagarina in the south

Soils: the Campo Rotaliano is a large, gravelly, sandy plain protected by mountains

Climate: the central Valdadige is semi-continental, with Lake Garda’s influence fading towards Trento

Speciality: the home of Teroldego

Wine style: Teroldego Rotaliano DOC — dark, fruity and savoury

💡 More than 80% of Trentino’s vineyards are on the floor and slopes of the Valdadige.

🍇 The Vallagarina

Location: south of Trento, extending to the Veneto border

Speciality: Marzemino, Enantio

Wine style: Trentino DOC Marzemino may only come from here; the Isera and Ziresi sub-zones make Marzemino Superiore

🎭 Marzemino is sung about in Mozart’s Don Giovanni

🌊 Valle dei Laghi and Val di Cembra

Valle dei Laghi: south-west of the Adige Valley, along the Sarca as it flows to Lake Garda; almost Mediterranean, mild enough for olives and lemons

Speciality: Nosiola

Wine style:
Vino Santo: Nosiola dried for 5-6 months and affected by noble rot, aged at least 3 years (most producers 7-10)
Val di Cembra: steep terraces of purple porphyry, with Müller Thurgau the most distinctive

💡 Without the Ora del Garda, the Nosiola grapes drying for Vino Santo would rot.

🏔️ Alto Adige’s winegrowing districts

❄️ Valle Isarco/Eisacktal (Italy’s northernmost)

Location: the valley of the Isarco as it flows from Bressanone to join the Adige near Bolzano

Altitude: some of Alto Adige’s highest vineyards

Climate: cooler than the south and often marginal, so vineyards are mostly south-facing

Soils: weathered schist, gneiss and slate (rich in mica and quartz)

Grapes:
🍇 Sylvaner: the star
🍇 Riesling, Müller Thurgau, Kerner

🏰 The Abbazia di Novacella lies near Bressanone.

Style: cool-climate whites from high altitude.

🏛️ Bolzano/Bozen

🍷 Santa Maddalena/St. Magdalener

Location: the slopes north of Bolzano
Grape: Schiava
Style: fuller and more structured than other Schiava appellations
Status: a sub-zone of Alto Adige DOC

🌄 Colli di Bolzano/Bozner Leiten

Location: the hills around Bolzano
Grape: Schiava
Status: a sub-zone of Alto Adige DOC

🔴 The home of Lagrein (Gries)

Bolzano is one of Italy’s hottest areas (a basin at the foot of the Alps)
Lagrein Dunkel (dark) and Lagrein Kretzer (rosé)

🌤️ Bassa Atesina/Unterland

Location: the southernmost district, with vineyards on both banks of the Adige; main towns Cortaccia, Termeno/Tramin, Montagna, Egna and Magré

Climate: the driest part of Alto Adige; soils of limestone and dolomite

Grapes:
🍇 Gewürztraminer: historic home in Termeno and Cortaccia
🍇 Pinot Nero: best around Egna and Montagna
🍇 Müller Thurgau, Pinot Grigio

Style: warmer in the south, where Bordeaux varieties also ripen more easily.

🌊 Oltradige/Überetsch

Location: north of the Bassa Atesina on the right bank of the Adige; considered the heart of Alto Adige winegrowing

Key areas: Lake Caldaro (Lago di Caldaro) and the town of Appiano, two of the region’s largest growing areas

Grapes:
🍇 Schiava: the district’s best known
🍇 Pinot Bianco: at its best around Appiano

🌊 Lago di Caldaro DOC takes its name from the lake here.

Style: Bordeaux varieties are grown mainly here and in the Bassa Atesina.

⛰️ Altitude and grape placement

Valley floor
Trentino floor at 200-300 m
More fertile alluvial soils; Alto Adige’s three valley floors are mostly apple orchards
Lower slopes
Bolzano, Bassa Atesina, Oltradige
Red grapes go on the valley floor or lower slopes where possible, so they ripen
Mid to upper slopes
Val d'Adige, Terlano
White grapes on cooler, higher sites, for bright aromatics and vibrant acidity
800-1,000 m
Valle Isarco, Val Venosta, Val di Cembra
Cool high altitude: Sylvaner, Riesling, Kerner, Müller Thurgau

🌊 The Adige River

The Adige (German: Etsch), Italy’s second-longest river, rises in two Alpine lakes below the Resia Pass, runs through the Val Venosta, turns due south at Bolzano, crosses Trentino and flows through Veneto into the Adriatic.

🗺️ A “Y” shape: Alto Adige’s three valleys form a Y, with the Val Venosta and Valle Isarco as its arms
🌾 The main valley: Trentino’s Valdadige is about 65 km long, flanked by the Alps
🌬️ Ora del Garda: the breeze from Lake Garda reaches far north — Bolzano is less than 80 km from the lake
🪨 Alluvial soils: the gravels, sands and clays of Trentino’s valley floors come from glaciers, erosion and river deposits

slides.19.title: 🎓 Key Takeaways
slides.19.points.0: ✓ Trentino-Alto Adige is made up of two autonomous provinces that joined Italy in 1919; Alto Adige is mainly German-speaking, Trentino Italian-speaking
slides.19.points.1: ✓ Alto Adige is Italy’s northernmost wine region: a continental climate, about 300 days of sunshine, wide diurnal swings, and hillside vineyards at 200-1,000 m
slides.19.points.2: ✓ Alto Adige/Südtirol DOC varietal wines need at least 85% of the variety; its six sub-zones are Terlano, Valle Isarco, Santa Maddalena, Colli di Bolzano, Valle Venosta and Meranese
slides.19.points.3: ✓ The “Traminer” grown for centuries in Termeno/Tramin is actually Savagnin Blanc; Gewürztraminer is its aromatic mutation and Alto Adige’s third most planted grape
slides.19.points.4: ✓ Trento DOC (1993) was Italy’s first DOC exclusively for traditional method sparkling wine; time on lees: 15 months non-vintage, 24 vintage, 36 Riserva
slides.19.points.5: ✓ Teroldego, the “Prince of Trentino”, is native to the Campo Rotaliano; Teroldego Rotaliano DOC is 100% Teroldego, with Riserva aged at least 2 years
slides.19.points.6: ✓ Trentino has 8 DOCs (as of 2017) and over 80% of its wine is DOC; cooperatives, organised independently by growers, make about 75% of production
slides.19.points.7: ✓ The main training system is the Pergola Trentina; Vino Santo is made from dried Nosiola grapes and aged at least 3 years
slides.20.title: 🧠 Trentino-Alto Adige Knowledge Check
slides.20.questions.0.question: According to DNA research, what is the “Traminer” grown for centuries in Termeno/Tramin actually?
slides.20.questions.0.explanation: Traminer was long thought to originate in Termeno/Tramin, but the grape grown there for centuries is actually Savagnin Blanc; Gewürztraminer is its aromatic, pink-berried mutation (Savagnin Rose). Today only Gewürztraminer is grown in Alto Adige.
slides.20.questions.1.question: Which production method is used for Trento DOC?
slides.20.questions.1.explanation: Trento DOC covers all traditional method (Metodo Classico) sparkling wines made in Trentino. Created in 1993, it was the first Italian DOC dedicated exclusively to traditional method sparkling wine.
slides.20.questions.2.question: Which is Trentino’s most representative red grape?
slides.20.questions.2.explanation: Teroldego, the “Prince of Trentino”, is Trentino’s most important red grape and is native to the Campo Rotaliano; Teroldego Rotaliano DOC is 100% Teroldego.
slides.20.questions.3.question: Which empire did Alto Adige belong to before 1919?
slides.20.questions.3.explanation: Alto Adige was acquired by the House of Habsburg in the 14th century and remained linked to Austria until the end of World War I; it was ceded to the Kingdom of Italy in 1919.
slides.20.questions.4.question: What is the minimum time on lees for Trento DOC Riserva?
slides.20.questions.4.explanation: Trento DOC requires at least 15 months on lees for non-vintage wines, 24 months for vintage (millesimato) and 36 months for Riserva, which must be a vintage wine.
slides.20.questions.5.question: What are the main soils of the Valle Isarco/Eisacktal?
slides.20.questions.5.options.1: B. Weathered schist, gneiss and slate
slides.20.questions.5.explanation: The Valle Isarco is dominated by weathered schist, gneiss and slate rich in mica and quartz; limestone and dolomite are found in the Bassa Atesina in the south.
slides.20.questions.6.question: Which grape is Santa Maddalena/St. Magdalener dedicated to?
slides.20.questions.6.explanation: Santa Maddalena, on the slopes north of Bolzano, is a sub-zone of Alto Adige DOC and is considered the historic home of Schiava and its most prestigious zone of production.
slides.20.questions.7.question: What is the main traditional training system in Trentino and Alto Adige?
slides.20.questions.7.explanation: The Pergola Trentina is the traditional local overhead training system; since the 1990s vertical systems such as Guyot have become more common.
slides.20.questions.8.question: Which grape is used to make Trentino Vino Santo?
slides.20.questions.8.explanation: Vino Santo is made from Nosiola: the grapes are air-dried for 5-6 months in high, well-ventilated rooms and are affected by noble rot; the wine is aged at least 3 years, and most producers age it 7-10 years.
slides.20.questions.9.question: According to DNA research, Lagrein has a parent-offspring relationship with which grape?
slides.20.questions.9.explanation: DNA profiling has proven Lagrein to be an offspring of Teroldego; Teroldego in turn is related to Dureza, a parent of Syrah.
